# SDF-to-Brick Compiler & Greedy Mesher

Turning a 3D shape into a brick model you could really build takes three steps, the same ones digital brick tools such as the LDraw programs face:

1. **Fit the shape to the brick grid.** A brick is 8 mm across but 9.6 mm tall, so one layer up is 1.2 studs across. The shape is sampled into 1 × 1 cubes, one per stud per layer.
2. **Hollow it out**, if you like, keeping a skin one stud thick, as builders of big sculptures do to save bricks.
3. **Merge the cubes into real bricks**, 2 × 4 down to 1 × 1, a layer at a time. A real model also needs its joints *staggered*: each brick should sit across two below it, like bricks in a wall. Otherwise the joints line up into cracks that run up the model, and it falls apart in your hands.

C does all three and makes a parts list. three.js shows the model in 3D, and a plan view shows one layer from above with its joints.

How the cells run:

- **C runs in your browser.** The cell is compiled to WebAssembly by xcc, on the page, and runs at once, on the website too.
- **C reads the controls and shares its build.** `nb_get_int` reads the sculpture and settings, and `nb_set_json` shares the bricks with the views below. After changing the sculpture, joints or core, press **▶** on the C cell; the cut-plane slider works straight away.

> ✨ The code cells were written by an AI model from prompts, and each prompt is saved in its cell: press **✨** in a cell's header to see it.

Press **Run all**.

## 1. Choose a sculpture

> Controls, 920 pixels wide, titled "Brick Compiler & Layer Inspector": a dropdown "3D Sculpture (SDF)" bound to brick_model (0 a duck, 1 a castle keep, 2 a hollow dome, 3 a torus ring), default 0; a dropdown "Layer Seam Strategy" bound to brick_stagger (1 staggered joints, 0 plain greedy), default 1; a dropdown "Core Mode" bound to brick_hollow (1 hollow shell, 0 solid), default 1; and a slider "Live Cut-Plane Layer" bound to brick_cut_layer, 1 to 14, default 14.

## 2. Compile the shape into bricks

> In C, turn a 3D shape into toy bricks on a grid 16 × 16 studs and 14 layers high. Read the shape (brick_model: 0 a duck, 1 a castle keep, 2 a striped dome, 3 a torus), brick_stagger and brick_hollow from nb with <nb.h>. Sample the shape with distance and solid tests into coloured 1 × 1 cubes, scaling height by 1.2, because a brick is 9.6 mm tall and 8 mm wide. When hollow, remove every cube whose six neighbours are all filled. Then merge each layer's cubes of the same colour into bricks from 2 × 4 down to 1 × 1, biggest first; when staggering, turn the preferred direction 90° each layer and avoid joints that sit right above a joint in the layer below, even if that means a smaller brick. Print the cube and brick counts, the share of bricks that sit across two or more bricks below, and the parts list, and share nb.brick_build: {gx, gy, gz, rawVoxels, carvedVoxels, brickCount, interlockPct, bom, bricks: [[x, y, z, sx, sz, colour]]}.

- **`sample_sculpture`** answers "is there plastic here, and what colour?" for each cube. The duck's body is an ellipsoid, the dome a shell between two spheres, the torus a ring; `* 1.2` stretches height to match a brick.
- **The hollowing loop** removes any cube with all six neighbours filled, so only the outer skin is left.
- **`aligned_joints`** counts how much of a brick's edge would sit right above a joint in the layer below. When staggering, each brick scores 4 per stud minus 6 per lined-up joint, so a 1 × 3 that spans a joint can beat a 1 × 4 that doesn't.
- **`owner`** records which brick covers each stud. It's how the code knows where the joints below are, and how it scores the interlock.

## What the run shows

- **The duck takes 108 bricks.** It samples to 540 cubes; hollowing removes 188 of them, and the 352 left merge into 20 2 × 4s, 18 1 × 4s, 25 1 × 2s, 35 1 × 1s and a few others.
- **Staggering closes the cracks.** On the hollow castle keep, plain greedy lines up every joint on most layers (layer 8: 14 of 14), while staggered joints line up 1 of 19. The share of bricks that sit across two below rises from 4.8% to 49.5%, or from 1.6% to 70.1% when the castle is solid.
- **It costs a few bricks.** The staggered castle needs 352 bricks against 334, and the solid duck 113 against 95.
- **Curved skins hardly bond at all.** The hollow duck has almost no lined-up joints, yet only 14.7% of its bricks sit across two below, and the torus 0.5%. A skin one stud thick that curves moves sideways every layer, so most bricks rest on a single brick or hang over the edge. Solid shapes bond far better: the duck reaches 58% and the dome 59%.
- **Hollowing saves plastic, not bricks.** The hollow duck has 35% fewer studs than the solid one, but 108 bricks against 113.

## Try this

Each of these is a prompt. Press **✨** in a cell's header to change its prompt and generate it again, or **⚡ AI Generate New Cell** at the bottom to add a new one.

- **See the cracks.** Choose the castle keep and **Plain greedy**, press **▶** on the C cell, and set the cut plane to 8. The plan view fills with red; switch back to staggered joints and run it again.
- **A bigger brick.** Press ✨ on the C cell and add: *"Add the 2 × 6 brick (part 2456) to the catalogue, ahead of the 2 × 4."* Does the solid duck need fewer bricks?
- **Your own sculpture.** Press ✨ on the C cell and add: *"Add a fifth shape, model 4: a lighthouse with red and white stripes and a yellow lamp at the top."* Then press ✨ on the controls and add it to the sculpture list.
- **Bricks per layer.** New JavaScript cell: *"Read nb.brick_build and return a Vega-Lite stacked bar chart of the bricks on each layer, coloured by size (2×4, 2×3 and so on)."*
- **Understand the code.** Press the speech bubble (**Explain this cell**) on the C cell and ask how `aligned_joints` decides between a 1 × 4 and a 1 × 3.
